newsitem.title: NETHERLANDS: FOCUS - Unisource losses widen, break even in view.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS - Unisource losses widen, break even in view.

text.p: European telecoms joint venture Unisource said on Tuesday its 1996 losses widened, mainly due to non-recurring expansion costs, but said it was on track to break even by 2000 as revenues soar.
Unisource, which groups Koninklijke PTT Nederland, Telia of Sweden and Swiss Telecom said its losses increased in 1996 to 375.4 million guilders from 319.7 million in 1995.

"We are now on the upward track to break-even," Unisource finance director Jan de Vries said in a statement. "The company expects a ten billion guilder revenue by the turn of the century, by which time break-even will be reached," he said.

Unisource, established in 1992 and headquartered at Hoofddorp near Amsterdam, booked revenues of 2.43 billion guilders in 1996, up 85 percent on the year before as demand for international telephone services continued to explode.

Chief executive Paul Smits said in an interview with Reuters that after five years, Unisource had established a European company which is rapidly growing and is only in a beginning phase of exploiting its opportunities.
"In that respect I would call (it) successful," Smits said.
The group said revenues in 1996 were particularly boosted by the acquisition of business telecoms and data transmission firm Unisource Espana from former partner Telefonica.

Telefonica was asked to leave Unisource in April by the remaining three partners after the Spanish company formed an alliance with a rival grouping of British Telecommunications Plc and MCI of the United States, but Smits said Unisource was in no hurry to seek a replacement.
"We are not actively looking to a partner in the respect that we desperately have to find a partner because something's missing. New partners have to bring something to us," he said.
Growth in home country markets and other European target markets such as Belgium, France, Germany and Italy also contributed to the increase in revenues.

The groups said losses deepened as the group continued with "significant" investments, particularly in the further expansion of its international backbone network and in costs related to new communications services in Europe.

Unisource said a significant part of the costs it had were non-recurring, although costs were only offset to a limited extent by an increase in revenue from international voice communications, owing to the long sales cycle of the segment.
Smits said Unisource was heading for substantial revenue growth in 1997 and the company aimed to shorten the time needed to bring new services to market and cut sales cycle times.
"The good news is that in many aspects 1996 is the last year of what we call the foundation years, and also the last year where investments are preceeding results," he said.
"From 1996 onwards we will show...improving bottom lines, it's a kind of a milestone as we see it," Smits said.
